title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Sleep — October 2026

studies.title: Bad nights and next-day eating disorder symptoms feed each other in a daily loop
studies.ns_score_reason: pre-registered, intensively sampled real-world data on a hard-to-study clinical group; limited by self-report and the absence of objective sleep measurement.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers at the University of Louisville recruited 128 people meeting criteria for anorexia nervosa spectrum disorders who had current or past suicidal ideation, and had them complete repeated daily smartphone surveys (ecological momentary assessment) about sleep, eating disorder behaviors and suicidal thoughts. In pre-registered multilevel models, a night of disturbed sleep predicted more restriction, binge eating, compensatory behaviors, body checking and suicidal ideation the following day — and each of those symptoms, in turn, predicted a worse night's sleep. The effects ran in both directions within the same person, day after day.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes poor sleep in eating disorders as an active part of the machinery that keeps symptoms going, rather than a side effect of being unwell — and suggests sleep may be one lever that touches both eating pathology and suicide risk at once. It is still correlational within-person data, so it marks out a target for trials rather than proving one.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the ordinary texture of a bad night — 3am, counting hours until morning — and the finding that for people with anorexia the next day is measurably harder, and that the hard day then wrecks the next night. The hook is a closed loop detected in real time, not retrospectively, in a group whose daily life is rarely captured this way. Call Cheri Levinson's lab at Louisville, which runs this kind of momentary-assessment work, and ask what an experimental test of the loop would look like.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for a health or psychiatry-focused outlet on the rise of ecological momentary assessment as a way of studying symptoms that only exist in the flow of a day — how smartphone diaries are quietly replacing the clinic questionnaire, and what gets lost and gained when psychiatry measures people hourly.
studies.caveats: Observational design — temporal precedence is not causation; all measures self-reported with no actigraphy or polysomnography; N=128 in a specific clinical population (ANSD with suicidality) that may not generalize; no control group of unaffected sleepers.

studies.title: Sleep helps the brain file away where things were, in both directions at once
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, theory-driven test of what exactly sleep consolidates, though it extends an established hypothesis rather than overturning it, and sample size is not reported in the abstract.
studies.the_study: Psychologists at the University of Mannheim showed participants pictures to memorize, each appearing at a particular horizontal and vertical position on screen — positions nobody was told to learn. After a gap filled either by a night of natural sleep or a day of wakefulness, participants were tested on where each image had been. Using multinomial modeling to separate genuine binding from guessing, the team found sleep improved memory not just for an item and one piece of context, but for the item plus *both* spatial dimensions bound together.
studies.why_it_matters: It sharpens the active systems consolidation account of sleep: the sleeping brain does not merely strengthen individual associations but knits together separate, incidentally noticed features of a scene into a single retrievable package. That is close to what we colloquially mean by an episodic memory.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the oddity that you remember *where* something was without ever trying to — and that a night's sleep makes that accidental knowledge more coherent, not just stronger. Open on the everyday experience of recalling the position of a paragraph on a page days later. Worth calling Beatrice Kuhlmann or Edgar Erdfelder at Mannheim; Erdfelder's multinomial modeling approach is the methodological hook for why this result is more than "sleep is good for memory."
studies.wider_angle: A feature for an education or learning-focused outlet on why context matters for recall — the revision-timing question of whether spacing study before sleep changes what kind of memory you end up with, and how far the lab evidence actually supports the sleep-and-study advice already circulating online.
studies.caveats: Sample size not stated in the abstract; laboratory task with incidental spatial context may not map onto rich real-world memory; sleep versus wake comparison confounds time of day with sleep itself, a known limitation of this design; single-center.

studies.title: Anxiety about keeping up with AI tracks with worse sleep
studies.ns_score_reason: extremely timely and relatable, but a cross-sectional mediation model in a self-selected sample can only establish that these worries travel together.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Yildiz Technical University in Istanbul surveyed 364 adults aged 18 to 60 (72 percent women, mean age 28) about "AI competence anxiety" — worry about whether one's skills will keep pace with artificial intelligence — alongside measures of repetitive negative thinking, anxiety about the future and sleep disturbance. Using structural equation modeling with bootstrapped indirect effects, and controlling for age, sex and how often people used AI tools, they found AI competence anxiety was linked to disturbed sleep indirectly, via rumination and then future anxiety in sequence.
studies.why_it_matters: It is an early attempt to measure a worry that a lot of people report anecdotally and to specify the route by which it might reach the bedroom — through chewing things over, rather than directly. Right now it opens a line of enquiry rather than establishing that AI anxiety costs anyone sleep.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that the worry doesn't appear to keep people awake on its own — it does so, statistically, only after it has been converted into rumination and then dread about the future, which is exactly the chain that existing insomnia therapies already target. Open on a mid-career professional lying awake wondering whether their job survives the next model release. Call Begüm Ceren Kara's group at Yildiz Technical University, and pair them with a cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia researcher who can say whether this is just old-fashioned worry wearing new clothes.
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece for a work or technology outlet on the psychology of technological obsolescence — how employers are measuring and managing "AI anxiety," what previous waves of automation anxiety did to workers' health, and whether reskilling programs help or heighten the dread.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional data, so the mediation sequence is a statistical model, not a demonstrated temporal process; all outcomes self-reported; sample skewed female, young and Turkish — may not generalize; N=364 is adequate for the model but modest; no clinical sleep assessment.

studies.title: Religious practice goes with lighter sleep problems in older women, but not men — and the link mostly dissolves on adjustment
studies.ns_score_reason: large national sample and a useful corrective to "sleep gets worse with age" framing, but the headline association is attenuated to non-significance once psychosocial factors are accounted for, which is itself the honest story.
studies.the_study: Using the 2018 Longitudinal Study of Aging and Health in Vietnam (n=4901, aged 60 and over), researchers at Chulalongkorn University used latent class analysis on six self-reported sleep indicators and found three distinct profiles: mild (29.4 percent), moderate (45.6 percent) and severe (25.0 percent). Notably, the moderate and severe groups reported similarly high insomnia symptoms but diverged sharply on perceived sleep quality, restfulness and medication use. Religious and spiritual engagement was associated with a 6 percentage-point higher chance of falling into the mild group among women — an association that shrank and lost significance after adjusting for psychosocial and behavioral factors — with no association at all among men.
studies.why_it_matters: The more interesting result is the sleep typology: two people can report identical insomnia symptoms and have completely different subjective experiences of their nights, which argues against treating "poor sleep in old age" as one thing. The religion finding looks less like a protective effect of belief and more like a proxy for social connection and daily routine.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the mediation that undoes the headline — the apparent benefit of religious engagement for older women's sleep largely disappears once you account for social and behavioral life, hinting that what's doing the work is company and structure, not faith. Open on the early-morning pagoda routine of an older Vietnamese woman. Call Wiraporn Pothisiri at Chulalongkorn's College of Population Studies, and ask why no equivalent pattern shows up in men.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest or global-health outlet on how sleep complaints are described and treated outside wealthy Western countries — where sleeping-pill use, insomnia labels and what counts as a "restful" night all look different, and what that implies for the globalizing sleep-health industry.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional analysis of a single survey wave — cannot establish causation or direction; all sleep measures self-reported with no objective assessment; the key association is non-significant in the fully adjusted model; residual confounding likely; findings specific to older Vietnamese adults.

studies.title: One in four drug users in a Spanish survey say they take something to help them sleep
studies.ns_score_reason: a big dataset with a genuinely under-reported angle (self-medication for sleep and mood, and chemsex spreading beyond men who have sex with men), but it is a self-selected web survey and sleep is a secondary finding.
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed responses from 6399 people in Spain who completed the European Web Survey on Drugs 2024, examining why and where people use drugs. While recreational use dominated (78 percent), substantial minorities reported using cannabis or heroin to relax or manage stress (49.7 percent and 30.1 percent respectively), to improve sleep (26.7 percent) and to cope with anxiety or depression (26.4 percent). Use of drugs to enhance sex was reported by 13.7 percent; chemsex specifically by 3.3 percent, historically concentrated among men who have sex with men but increasingly reported by women.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents how much illicit drug use in a European country is functioning as unsupervised self-medication for insomnia and distress rather than as recreation — a framing largely absent from drug policy, which treats use as a leisure behavior. It also provides one of the first population-level signals that chemsex is no longer an exclusively MSM phenomenon.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is how much of Europe's illicit drug use looks like untreated insomnia and anxiety: a quarter of respondents said they used to get to sleep. Open on someone who started using cannabis nightly because they couldn't get an appointment for their insomnia. Call the Observatorio Español de las Drogas y las Adicciones, which co-authored the analysis, and ask whether waiting lists for sleep and mental health care map onto these patterns.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist health-policy or LGBTQ+ outlet: the shifting demographics of chemsex, and whether harm-reduction services designed almost entirely around men who have sex with men are equipped for the women now reporting it.
studies.caveats: Self-selected online convenience sample — not population-representative, and likely to over-sample engaged or heavier users; cross-sectional and entirely self-reported; reasons for use are retrospective self-attributions; sleep is a secondary finding, not the study's focus; one author declares multiple pharmaceutical lecture fees and commercial interests (Takeda, BIAL, Rubio, Rovi), though unrelated to this dataset.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- "Quality" keeps fracturing into several different things. The latent class analysis in "Religious practice goes with lighter sleep problems in older women" (PMID 42838779) finds moderate and severe classes reporting near-identical insomnia symptoms but sharply divergent perceived restfulness and medication use — the same disjunction between symptom counts and subjective experience that drove "It's how well you sleep, not how long, that tracks your heart and metabolic risk" (PMID 42648984) and that left "Night owls don't actually sleep worse than larks" (PMID 42751860) with a clean phase difference and a null on quality.
- Technology reaches sleep through how it is experienced, not how much of it there is. "Anxiety about keeping up with AI tracks with worse sleep" (PMID 42830665) routes its effect through rumination and future anxiety rather than directly, echoing "How you use your phone predicts depression far better than how long you use it" (PMID 42759324), where problematic use outperformed hours and sleep sat awkwardly between the two patterns.
- Person-centered clustering continues to displace composite scoring: the three-class sleep typology in PMID 42838779 uses the same logic as the latent profile analysis that isolated a poor-sleep/low-activity cluster in "Poor sleep and inactivity cluster together" (PMID 42723029).
- Headline associations that dissolve on adjustment appear in both runs: the religious-engagement benefit for older Vietnamese women attenuates to non-significance (PMID 42838779), much as the short-sleep mortality signal vanished after adjustment in "Sleeping nine hours or more is linked to earlier death" (PMID 42744622).

**Advances**
- "Bad nights and next-day eating disorder symptoms feed each other in a daily loop" (PMID 42834479) pushes intensive within-person temporal modeling from infant sleep into clinical psychiatry. "Camera-tracked cribs reveal how a baby's temperament locks in their sleep pattern" (PMID 42470789) separated night-to-night variability from inertia in babies; this new study applies daily lagged modeling to an adult clinical population with suicidality, and tests both directions rather than one.
- "Sleep helps the brain file away where things were, in both directions at once" (PMID 42844862) supplies controlled human evidence on exactly the function that "Honeybees nap in bursts all day, and their sleep may hold a lesson for AI" (PMID 42728400) argued invertebrates were the right place to test — binding of incidental context, not just strengthening of single associations.

**Counterpoints**
- The two batches rest on very different measurement bases. September's digest was instrumentation-heavy — actigraphy (PMIDs 42751860, 42637627), split-night polysomnography with pulse transit time (PMID 42754769), structural MRI (PMID 42202661), crib computer vision (PMID 42470789). Every study in this batch is self-reported sleep, including the momentary-assessment loop in PMID 42834479, which has temporal resolution but no objective sleep measure at all. Any apparent agreement across runs should be read with that in mind.
- Directionality: previous lagged and genetic work had been converging on one-way sleep-to-symptom effects. PMID 42834479 reports a reciprocal within-person loop in anorexia spectrum disorders, which cuts against that tidying-up — though with self-report on both sides of the equation.

**New themes**
- Self-medication and the treatment gap arrive for the first time: "One in four drug users in a Spanish survey say they take something to help them sleep" (PMID 42802253), with medication use also a distinguishing feature of the severe sleep class in PMID 42838779.
- AI changes role. In September it was an instrument or an analogy — ECG apnea detection (PMID 42747635), bees as a template for catastrophic forgetting (PMID 42728400). Here it is a psychological exposure in its own right (PMID 42830665).
- Non-Western ageing cohorts: PMID 42838779 is the first study in these runs to characterize sleep complaints in an older low- and middle-income population on their own terms rather than as a comparison to US or UK data.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four of the five studies describe what people do about bad nights when no clinician is involved. A quarter of respondents to Spain's arm of the European Web Survey on Drugs said they used illicit drugs to sleep, and roughly half used cannabis to relax (PMID 42802253); in Vietnam, medication use and perceived restfulness — not insomnia symptoms — separated the moderate from the severe sleep class, while religious and social routine tracked with the mildest class until adjustment absorbed the effect (PMID 42838779); AI competence anxiety reached the bedroom only after passing through rumination and future dread, the exact chain that cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is built to interrupt (PMID 42830665); and in anorexia spectrum disorders a disturbed night and the next day's symptoms escalate each other in a closed loop nobody is currently treating as a sleep problem (PMID 42834479).

**Why pitch this now:** CBT-I is first-line in essentially every national guideline and is available to almost nobody, and these papers independently document the substitutes filling that vacuum — cannabis, hypnotics, daily structure, religious routine — in three countries and across three very different populations.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the informal economy of sleep: who actually treats insomnia, what people reach for when they can't get an appointment, and why the mechanism these studies keep landing on — nighttime rumination — is the one thing the unavailable therapy is best at fixing. For general readers who have lain awake and improvised, with enough health-policy spine to interest commissioners of services.

**Potential headlines:**
- Most insomnia is being treated outside the health system
- It isn't the worry that keeps you awake, it's turning it over
- What people reach for at 3am when there is no insomnia clinic

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the mechanism-plus-access framing suits the magazine's appetite for a human behavior story with a clear causal chain underneath it.
- **The Guardian science desk** — self-medication as a drug-policy story as much as a sleep story, with a strong UK peg on CBT-I waiting lists and hypnotic prescribing.
- **STAT** — the guideline-versus-availability gap for a first-line behavioral therapy is squarely its health-systems beat.
- **Undark** — for the comparative edge: how insomnia is named, medicated and endured in Vietnam and Spain versus the Anglo-American sleep-health market.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Sleep — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-10 | **Studies reviewed:** 5
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

### Study 1: Bad nights and next-day eating disorder symptoms feed each other in a daily loop
**PMID:** 42834479 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core facts check out: N=128, ANSD with current or past suicidal ideation, daily EMA, pre-registered hypotheses and analyses, multilevel models, bidirectional lagged associations across restriction, binge eating, compensatory behaviors, body checking and SI. Framing is appropriately non-causal and the caveats are honest.

**Issue A. Institutional attribution is incomplete** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Researchers at the University of Louisville recruited 128 people"
- **Abstract says:** Authors are affiliated with the University of Louisville (Buseman, Cash, Levinson) and Auburn University (Smith AR, Department of Psychological Sciences).
- **Problem:** The study is a multi-institution collaboration; Auburn is dropped.
- **Suggested fix:** "Researchers at the University of Louisville, with a collaborator at Auburn University, recruited 128 people"

**Issue B. "Smartphone surveys" is not stated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "had them complete repeated daily smartphone surveys (ecological momentary assessment)"
- **Abstract says:** "completed daily ecological momentary assessment (EMA) surveys"
- **Problem:** The delivery method (smartphone) is plausible but not specified. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "had them complete repeated daily ecological momentary assessment surveys"

**Issue C. NS fit score sits slightly high for all-self-report EMA data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10"
- **Abstract says:** All constructs — sleep disturbance, ED symptoms, SI — are self-reported via EMA; no objective sleep measure, no comparison group.
- **Problem:** A 7 rests on data that are entirely self-reported and uncontrolled, even if pre-registered and intensively sampled. The pre-registration and clinical-population access are real strengths, but the evidence does not support a 7.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — pre-registered, intensively sampled real-world data on a hard-to-study clinical group; limited by self-report throughout, absence of objective sleep measurement and no comparison group."

*Note:* "The effects ran in both directions within the same person" — the abstract tested both within- and between-person effects but does not specify at which level each significant effect emerged. Unverifiable from abstract only; worth checking the full text before the pitch leans on "within the same person."

---

### Study 2: Sleep helps the brain file away where things were, in both directions at once
**PMID:** 42844862 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Method description (intentionally learned pictures, incidentally learned horizontal and vertical screen positions, natural night sleep vs daytime wakefulness, multinomial modelling, bound source memory benefit), institution and journal details all match. The caveat correctly notes sample size is absent from the abstract.

**Issue A. "First-in-class" novelty label conflicts with the abstract's own framing** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** First-in-class"
- **Abstract says:** "Extending previous research on sleep benefits in item-context associative memory, we investigated whether sleep also improves bound source memory for cross-dimensional context associations."
- **Problem:** The authors position this as an extension of an established literature and a confirmation of the active systems consolidation hypothesis, not a first-of-its-kind result. The NS fit note already concedes this ("extends an established hypothesis rather than overturning it"), so the novelty tag contradicts the digest's own assessment.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Incremental extension — first test of cross-dimensional context binding"

---

### Study 3: Anxiety about keeping up with AI tracks with worse sleep
**PMID:** 42830665 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=364, ages 18–60, 71.98% female, mean age 28.43, Yildiz Technical University, two-step SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects, controls for gender, age and AI tool usage frequency — all accurate. Headline is correctly non-causal and the caveats are strong.

**Issue A. Pitch claims a null direct effect the abstract never reports** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The surprise is that the worry doesn't appear to keep people awake on its own — it does so, statistically, only after it has been converted into rumination and then dread about the future"
- **Abstract says:** "The results indicated significant indirect associations between artificial intelligence competence anxiety and sleep disturbance through RNT and future anxiety."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports significant *indirect* effects; it says nothing about whether the direct path was non-significant. "Doesn't keep people awake on its own" and "only after" assert full mediation, which cannot be established from the abstract. This is the hook of the pitch, so it needs to hold.
- **Suggested fix:** "The hook is the route: the link between AI competence anxiety and disturbed sleep runs statistically through repetitive negative thinking and then anxiety about the future — the same chain existing insomnia therapies already target. (Check the full text for whether a direct effect survived.)"

**Issue B. "Rumination" substituted for repetitive negative thinking** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "linked to disturbed sleep indirectly, via rumination and then future anxiety in sequence"
- **Abstract says:** "repetitive negative thinking (RNT)"
- **Problem:** RNT is a broader construct than rumination (it includes worry and post-event processing); swapping the term narrows the finding and may misdescribe the instrument used.
- **Suggested fix:** "linked to disturbed sleep indirectly, via repetitive negative thinking and then future anxiety in sequence"

**Issue C. Author's first name not verifiable** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Begüm Ceren Kara's group at Yildiz Technical University"
- **Abstract says:** "Kara BC"
- **Problem:** The expanded given name is an inference from initials. Unverifiable from abstract only — confirm before the pitch goes out.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call B. C. Kara's group at Yildiz Technical University" (pending name confirmation)

---

### Study 4: Religious practice goes with lighter sleep problems in older women, but not men — and the link mostly dissolves on adjustment
**PMID:** 42838779 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Dataset (2018 LSAHV), n=4901, age ≥60, Chulalongkorn University, six self-reported indicators, three latent classes at 29.4 / 45.6 / 25.0 percent, the moderate–severe contrast, the 6.0 percentage-point female association and the null result in men are all reported correctly. Non-causal language throughout; caveats accurate.

**Issue A. "Mostly dissolves" overstates the attenuation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the link mostly dissolves on adjustment"
- **Abstract says:** "This association was attenuated by 2.0 percentage points after further adjustment for psychosocial and behavioral factors and was no longer statistically significant."
- **Problem:** The point estimate fell from 6.0 to roughly 4.0 percentage points — a reduction of about a third, not "mostly." What vanished was statistical significance, not most of the effect size. Readers will take "mostly dissolves" to mean the estimate collapsed.
- **Suggested fix:** "...and the link loses statistical significance on fuller adjustment"

**Issue B. Sequential adjustment described as a mediation analysis** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Lead with the mediation that undoes the headline — the apparent benefit of religious engagement for older women's sleep largely disappears once you account for social and behavioral life, hinting that what's doing the work is company and structure, not faith."
- **Abstract says:** Sex-stratified multinomial logistic regression with staged adjustment; attenuation of 2.0 percentage points after adding psychosocial and behavioral covariates. No mediation analysis is reported.
- **Problem:** Attenuation on covariate adjustment is suggestive of confounding or mediation, but the study did not test a mediation pathway, and a cross-sectional design could not separate the two. Calling it "the mediation" and concluding what is "doing the work" asserts a mechanism the analysis cannot deliver — and "largely disappears" repeats the Issue A overstatement.
- **Suggested fix:** "Lead with what happens on adjustment: the association between religious engagement and milder sleep problems in older women shrinks and loses significance once psychosocial and behavioral factors are in the model — raising the question of whether company and routine, rather than faith itself, are carrying the signal. Note the design cannot separate confounding from mediation."

*Note:* "diverged sharply on perceived sleep quality, restfulness and medication use" — the abstract says only "differed in." Not flagged separately, but "sharply" is the digest's word, not the authors'.

---

### Study 5: One in four drug users in a Spanish survey say they take something to help them sleep
**PMID:** 42802253 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Headline and pitch generalize a cannabis/heroin-specific figure to all drug users** — Severity: Major

- **As written:** "One in four drug users in a Spanish survey say they take something to help them sleep" / "a quarter of respondents said they used to get to sleep"
- **Abstract says:** "Cannabis and heroin were frequently used to relax or manage stress (49.73% and 30.14%, respectively), improve sleep (26.66%), and cope with anxiety and/or depression (26.35%)."
- **Problem:** The 26.66 percent figure sits inside a sentence specifically about cannabis and heroin, and the abstract does not state that it refers to all 6,399 respondents or to all substances. The headline ("drug users... take something") and the pitch ("a quarter of respondents") both convert a substance-specific reason-for-use figure into a survey-wide prevalence. The body text handles this correctly ("using cannabis or heroin... to improve sleep (26.7 percent)"), which makes the headline and pitch internally inconsistent with the digest's own study description. This is the entire hook of the pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "A quarter of cannabis and heroin use in a Spanish survey was reported as a sleep aid." Pitch: "The surprise is how much cannabis and heroin use is reported as self-medication: roughly a quarter of it to get to sleep, a quarter to cope with anxiety or depression." Confirm the denominator from the full text before pitching.

**Issue B. "Population-level signal" contradicts the digest's own caveat** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It also provides one of the first population-level signals that chemsex is no longer an exclusively MSM phenomenon."
- **Abstract says:** "We analyzed data from 6,399 valid participants residing in Spain who completed the European Web Survey on Drugs... Though historically associated with MSM, chemsex use is increasingly reported among women."
- **Problem:** The European Web Survey on Drugs is a self-selected web survey, as the caveats correctly state ("not population-representative"). The body text asserts exactly the opposite. Separately, "one of the first" is unverifiable from the abstract, and the abstract's own conclusion still frames chemsex as "particularly among MSM."
- **Suggested fix:** "It also adds a large-survey signal — though from a self-selected sample — that chemsex is increasingly reported by women as well as men who have sex with men."

**Issue C. "Rather than as recreation" reverses the abstract's headline conclusion** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It documents how much illicit drug use in a European country is functioning as unsupervised self-medication for insomnia and distress rather than as recreation"
- **Abstract says:** "Recreational use was the most common reason for drug consumption (78.01%)... Illicit drug use in Spain is predominantly recreational and typically occurs at home, festivals, or nightlife venues."
- **Problem:** The authors' explicit conclusion is that use is *predominantly recreational*. "Rather than as recreation" inverts that. The digest reports the 78 percent figure in the study description but then argues against it in "Why it matters."
- **Suggested fix:** "It documents a substantial minority of illicit drug use functioning as unsupervised self-medication for insomnia and distress, alongside the predominantly recreational use the authors report"

*Cleared:* The industry conflict of interest (Blasco-Fontecilla; Takeda, BIAL, Rubio, Rovi lecture fees) is correctly disclosed in the caveats. Journal, date, N and the 78.01 / 13.66 / 3.31 percent figures are accurate. NS fit of 4/10 is defensible.

---
